Good.

I was in Jamaica.

Yeah.

I loved it.
Yeah.
Stayed at a place.

Stay at a place called Apes Hill.
Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah.
We had villas, right on the golf course, so it was really nice.
That's fantastic.
Well, what did the villas cost?
Uh, there was three bedrooms.

So he knew everybody's name, by the way, Mike Svigen.
Okay.
No, so anyways, he.
So, you know I've got a place there, right?
What's that?
You know I've got a place in Barbados.
Right?
I did not know that.
Yeah.
At the crane.
Been there for 2020, over 20 years.
Nice.
And I've built a till a bunch.
What an interesting golf course.
Deep hill.
Yeah, yeah, we played it four days in a row.
It was beautiful.
Ah, fantastic.
All right, we'll catch up on Barbados, but I'll admit, Andy, good morning.
Hello.
Good morning.
How you doing?
We're good, how are you?
Yeah, I'm good, thank you.
Rob, nice to meet you.
Len and Brent, nice to meet you.
Yeah, Andy, I'll give you the super quick intro and you can delete all the vacation discussions in fireflies note taker that was there before you joined.
I.
So Len and Brent are my two partners.
The three of us own somewhere around 88% to 90% of the company.
Len was one of the original founders of.
He's the O in OKD, founded 43 years ago, and Brent joined him around twelve or 13 years ago.
And my agency, Brandfire, we merged with OKD in beginning of 2020 and formed the Evolve agency group.
And for the last four years, it's grown like stink.
Don't know if that's an expression outside of Canada or not in the UK.
No.
Well, it's a good thing.
I'm like, what does stink grow like?
No, I did delete that.
And we brought on board knowing, I think I shared this with you before.

We've had five or more unsolicited offers to buy the business years ago, going through due diligence with KPMG and whatnot, realized that to sell the agency for the most amount, we really want to build an executive team under us and, in essence, make ourselves irrelevant, which we've spent the last two years really, really focusing on moving all duties and responsibilities to our president, Ira Baptiste, her management team, including David Olnick, who's our managing director, and Len.
Brent and I in the last year have actually removed our titles.
So our titles right now are just founding partners.
And as I said to you before, our plan is to hit our EBITDA target of Len 4,000,003.8.
I'm going to say I'm going to be 3.8 this year.
And as he almost slipped out, he's also known as Mister conservative.
So we want to hit those numbers in our fiscal year, which is a January 31 year end.
And then our plan was to go to market right after that.
We have, as I said to you before, we met with eight firms in the last twelve months or so, including sts.
The guys that MSQ used, what are they again?
Madison Alley.
Madison Alleyde.
We've met with a generalist firm called Firepower.
We've met with.
That's the only generalist firm.
Every single other firm that we met with specializes in not just marketing, but primarily digitally focused marketing agencies.
We had, in essence come to a decision.
We haven't signed anything with anybody, but we had come to a decision of who we liked both from a communication standpoint, fee standpoint, because you guys are expensive, all of you guys.
I'm not saying capital a is any different than anybody else.
And Andy, you and I have already talked about fees and you've already made a very, very nice offer that puts you right in line with everybody else.
So there's no issue there.

And then I've shared with Len and Brent that my first experience with Capital A, with emails going into our Barracuda network as a no SPF record and then being asked to buy an agency, but that you and I had a really good chat and it was a good enough chat that it made me say to my two partners, we should chat with Andy.
The floor is now yours.
Oh great.
So yes, the SPF records.
Yeah, that's hilarious.
Thank you for that.
They were there, by the way.
I don't know why that came up.
So.
Yeah, well, thank you, Rob, for introducing me to the rest of your board.
Look, I think there is very small difference between a lot of the m and a advisories that are out there.
I think probably the one difference for us is that my experience is selling my own company as well.
And that's the first thing that I bring to the table.
My background is marketing and media.
And after I sold my company and I was sat twiddling my thumbs, I stumbled into m and a almost by accident.
So I've come at it from a founder's point of view, and that's kind of my, my big bring to the table in terms of what we can do.
There's a buyer out there for every company.
It's just really about getting the pricing right, getting the story right, and then it's a volume question.
You know, how many conversations can we have?

Because at the end of the day, it's usually about chemistry and getting the fit for the way that your culture has evolved in your company and finding a company with a good fit for your people to go to.
So one big difference that I will say that we have is the volume play.
And as you know, we contacted you about buying an agency.
That's because everybody that comes into our network and into our mailing list, we're putting opportunities in front of the right people.
So we have a platform, agencies Co.
It has 20,000 subscribers to our mailing list, but we also have a database of 130,000 marketing agency owners as well.
And they're just UK, us, Canada, and a bit of Australia and I, New Zealand.
So all english language buyers, 99% of the work we do is in the US, even though we're headquartered in the UK.
Most of my team is in New York and some in San Francisco.
So we're London, New York, San Francisco in terms of where our team is.
So that's kind of it, really, you know, it's, it kind of is a trial by fire.
Rob, I'm sure you've, you've been through this.
Well, all of you have been through it before.
It's something you're all experienced in, but happy to answer any questions if you want to understand what else we can offer versus everybody else.
Well, yeah, go ahead, Brent.
What are you seeing in terms of valuations in the market and how they've changed over the last in 2024?
So valuations are pretty solid.
I would say that there isn't a big change across sort of the last five years.
I think since private equity came into the mix, they kind of, I think they buoyed the multiples and they kind of solidified them a little bit.
I think what we have seen in the last couple of years is a bottleneck for private equity.
So they came in and kind of pushed prices up, which was really good.
Im talking about the bottom end of the market now.
So anything sort of less than 50 million in valuations.

So they pushed the prices up initially, but the last couple of years, they've, because of the stock market, pricing has dropped, and so their opportunity to exit has kind of stifled that sort of upper end of the lower end of the market, the middle market.
So price prices have come down.
They were really optimistic about three years ago.
So, you know where you might get a six or seven times multiple, you might be able to get an eight or nine.
So I would say maybe they've come down just a slight bit for better agencies.
But generally speaking, the market is pretty fixed.
So most agencies kind of sell between four to six.
The better ones, and the ones with higher EBITDA, where you guys are, would sell up to sort of six to eight.
And then really unique agencies or some sort of hot spaces would sell for 910.
Eleven, maybe more.
And again, none of that's really fixed.
And our job is to push those multiples as high as we can get.
And this is going back to my point about volume, Brent, what we want to do is get you under as many noses as possible and get two or three offers on the table at exactly the same time.
And that's really what we're looking to achieve, so that we can leverage one really interested party against another and get more cash upfront, a bigger multiple, etcetera, etcetera.
With a company like ours and you guys being based in England, but doing the majority of your business in the US, where historically, where have the offers come from?
Are they us based companies?
Are they english?
Are they international?
Who's buying right now, I guess is what my question is.
So we've done deals.
We've done deals across the UK and Europe and across the US as well.
And also in Israel.
Actually, we just closed the deal a couple of months ago.
In Israel, I would say virtually all the buyers are american.
There's just better access to capital right across the market from the bottom end with SBA loans.
And they have something similar in Canada as well, but government backed loans for businesses, for acquisitions, but also just the capital markets, they're really good, and they've got tons of money.
So, yeah, I would say mostly us deals.
We work on the buy side as well, then, just to let you know.
So we do actually work with clients that are looking to buy.
So some of our transactions are buy side, which means we get a good view on what people are offering as well.
Okay, makes sense.
Well, what kind of cash?
Like, what kind of deals?
I guess it depends on strategic buyer versus pE.
But what kind of upfront cash are you seeing right now?
So, yeah, every deal is slightly different, but I would say sort of that the starting position is always about around 50% upfront.
That is my experience.
Probably about 90% of the time.
We have had offers with lower cash upfront.
We've never accepted them.
But again, the art of negotiation is being able to get that up as high as possible.
So it does vary slightly.
For instance, a couple of days ago, we had an offer, it was at 3 million.
We wanted it to be close to four, and we got them up by half a million in cash upfront.
So, yeah, it varies, but it tends to be around that point.
And that usually is 50%.

We want it at 50% of the valuation, usually, which means you could get, on the same day, some other sort of sweeteners as well, which could include equity rollover in the holding company, et cetera, et cetera.
But in your case, if you guys all wanted to exit 100%, then we would be pushing for 50% or more of that in cash.
And then it's usually a three year earn out, but not always.
We had a client fairly recently based in Texas, actually, and they wanted to get out in twelve months.
And so they actually hit all of their targets that were set by the buyer at month nine.
So they got out in nine months, which was a pretty good deal.
Yeah.
Again, we're a little bit unique in that we do have a senior management team that.
And some of them, and some of them are actually shareholders too.
So any roled equity went in, they would have a very.
They would have skin in the skin of the skin in the game as well moving forward with that, not just employees.
So that would also benefit.
And again, Len, nothing's really set in stone.
I think, you know, you guys have done the work, which is pretty rare.
Most sort of founders still have some day to day, and that will usually hold up that earn out somehow.

If you guys really have all got out of the day today, and nobody needs you for anything at all, then it could be that we could push that cash upfront higher, because technically you're just investors and you're selling an asset.
So it could be that we push harder for more percentage of cash upfront and we'd be able to justify it.
Andy, what kind of timeline are you seeing for?
Like, how long does the process take from day one to getting to an Loi or even agreement?
So we have a process that runs as a six month process.
The last couple of deals that we've done have been pretty much bang on the day.
Actually, one went over by one day because it was the weekend.
They just can get it signed on a Friday.
So it's a six month process and it's totally doable.
You can actually do it quicker than that.
A lot of M and A advisors tend to say a year or more and lots of preparation and lots of slowing the process down, but it can be much quicker.
What tends to happen is if everybody is aligned, particularly on the sellers team, it can go really, really quickly.
If you've done the preparation.
There's, you know, as I said about the deal that we closed for nine months of an earn out, we actually found the buyer 30 days before they closed.
So it could have just been a 30 day process, but obviously we have to find lots of buyers.
You need to talk to people, et cetera, et cetera.
But we had an offer on the table and another buyer came in with a better offer and they closed within 30 days.
So it can be extremely quick.
So we also have a bit of a unique situation.
I don't know if Ralph filled you in on it, but we've gone through with an english company, a UK company, who were interested in acquiring us.
They acquired one of our partner companies who we were partners with, and that's how it sort of came about.
So we've gone through the process with them of providing them some fairly robust or detailed financial statements.

And that was done in early September, late August, and basically what they said to us was, okay, but let's get through your year end, because our numbers for our year end are going to look markedly different than they did in August based on confirmed spending.
So I guess my question is, if that offer was still to come to the table, how would your fees reflect that?
Because we still do not want to negotiate this on our own.
So if your fee is ten to do a full thing for us, if we said, here's an offer, deal with it, how would you charge us for that?
Before you answer, Andy, just to let you know, you've already given me those numbers.
Oh, okay.
Sorry.
Then I apologize.
That's okay.
Should I put you on the spot and see what your answer now is?
The same ones, then?
Whatever.
Whatever I told Rob last time is the same.
Okay.
Yeah.
So if you have a deal, then we have no claim to that at all.
So if you're happy to negotiate on your own, you know, it's a non exclusive agreement that we have.
We prefer to work exclusively, but actually our contract is a non exclusive agreement.
Even though we call it an exclusive agreement, it does have the stipulation that if you find your own deal, or it comes through a different broker, then, you know, we have no claim to that.
We have a win fee, which we've come down on, usually at 5%, but we are happy to lower that win fee if you have the deal already.
So, yeah, what you had said before.
Who wants us to negotiate it?
Yeah, you'll bring the fee down to three.
And if we have our own buyer, you'd bring it down to one and a half.
Yeah.
So we usually half it.
Yeah, yeah.
And that's.
That would only be, Len, if you wanted us to negotiate for you.
But again, yeah, if you wanted to negotiate yourself, then that would be, you know, no, no fees to us.
We would just step back, or even we would just continue with the process and try and find you a better offer.
A better offer.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.

And Len, go ahead and, and sorry to say this in front of Andy, but regardless is we have another option, which we haven't talked about, which is, again, if we wanted to put a third party in between us and that UK firm, it could also be our m and a lawyer that could, because part of the negotiations is going to be the deal terms, and it's the minutiae of the purchase agreement that we don't want to risk because we don't have experience in negotiating this level of detail of deal terms, whether we would look at having you help us with that or having our m and a lawyer help us with that.
So one and a half percent on.
Well, what I would say to that, Rob, is you would be better off if you had somebody that brought that deal to you and their experience in M and A allowing them to negotiate.
But I would just warn you on lawyers negotiate in business terms.
One, they are terrible at doing it.
Everything is, you know, fatal and scary when a lawyer deals, but also they're going to be charging you by the hour on top of that.
So sometimes that can really escalate fees and also just long it out for a much longer period of time.
Yeah, but, yeah, my experience is that lawyers are terrible at negotiating the business terms.
Once you have the business terms agreed, then that's the best time.
Even M and a lawyers, that's the best time to get them involved.
They tend to just over inflate the importance of absolutely every minor.
Yeah.
Because they make more money when they do that.
Unless they work on a fixed fee.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
The fixed fee.
I mean, I would suggest that you have a lawyer and a fixed fee fee anyway for agreeing the terms, but if you can get them on a fixed fee, I would say, yeah, you don't need us at all.
You could just get a lawyer to negotiate.
Just be mindful that they don't really understand the business terms.
It's always like it's black or white with them.
It's something that's going to be completely stupid that they can't agree to at all.
And it would just.
They tend to kill the deal, basically, is what I'm saying.
Yeah.
If you've got a good one, then who knows?
Yeah.
Andy, what is the, what is the, what does the process look like for marketing the agency?
Once we're, you know, once we say, yes, let's go.
I mean, because I'm a subscriber to theagencies Co.
I get the emails about, you know, new agencies.
I get your emails as well.
What does that look like?
And are you, is it simply a volume play or how do you work with the.
On the buy side to kind of match us up?
Yeah.
So there's kind of three levels to that.
So we have the sort of big fishing net that obviously you're part of that's going out to our agency's mailing list.
We also do a deep dive into our CRM, so we're matching keywords on keywords that we've created against your business.
So we're looking for.
Companies have a match in that.
So that's kind of the big sort of trawler going out and seeing if we can bring something home.
But then on top of that, we've got a more sniper approach where our team are basically researching the market and looking for those types of companies that have done these deals before.
So we're constantly finding new stuff.
Every client is slightly different.
So we're looking for an exact match somewhere that we haven't found them before.
And we always bring something up there as well.
So we've got this big long list, we've got more focus list.
And then myself and David Tsutsumi, who is our MD, who's based in San Francisco, we have great networks as well.
We're reaching out to our network to try and find.
So we've got these three different levels that are going on.
But, yeah, obviously there's a very, there's a very sort of broad volume play that we're doing amongst them.
We tend to find buyers in all of those sort of strata.
So we have to do them all.
Yeah.
Okay, great.
Is the process getting longer or shorter?
Are clients, you know, due diligence becoming tougher, easier?
What are you hearing on the closing process.
I wouldn't say that I'm seeing any real change in the process.
Obviously, there are some buyers or sellers that are super cautious and they hold up the process.
We're working on some buy side deals now, and our buyers are extremely experienced and they're very gung ho.
They're literally 2030 days to close very quickly, working through due diligence once they've made an offer.
So it just varies from deal to deal.
I think it just depends on both sides.
But personally, I haven't seen anything that's changed or where the process has been held up by new changes recently.
It's pretty much the same.
One thing we didn't add, I don't remember, I don't have it in my notes, is your fees relative to the terms of our payments.
So if we're getting half upfront and then a three year earn out or shares that we can't sell for a year or two, do your fees follow our cash flow?
No, they follow the valuation of the company.
So, yeah, this comes up every so often, particularly if you're bought by a listed company and they're giving you stock, for instance, and that stock's locked up for a year or two years.
Sometimes we basically get paid out on the valuation.
And my preference is obviously, Rob, on day one, which would look like on the cash at least, would look like a 6% rather than a 3%.
But it varies from deal to deal.

Again, sometimes our clients like to just get us out on day one as well, because you've got very nice terms on the ear now, it could be all, you know, it could have guaranteed payments plus some additional payments made on hitting targets, which would make our fee even bigger.
So some of our clients just like to just pay us out on day one and we walk away then.
So, yeah, preference is day one, but in reality, we sometimes wait every year up to three years.
I think the longest one we've had is five year deal where we still have some payments to come out.
Yeah.
Okay.
I mean, we'll figure out the tax situation and so on of that, but nice to know that you're flexible.
That, and by the way, everybody else we've spoken to that we're interested in hiring has also said that they'll be flexible to kind of match our cash flow.
The cash.
Yeah, yeah.
On the shares that does have a cash value.
And so if they're offered on day one, we usually get paid theme on those.
We've had that just recently, actually.
And the acquirer, which wasn't our client insisted on it, so we were quite happy about that.
Okay, tell us a little bit more about your team.
So yeah, fairly small team, like I said, based in the UK, New York and San Francisco really.
I mean we've got some juniors that are working for us, which I'm sure you will meet as well.
They'll be part of the process and onboarding, but sort of the important people are myself and David.
So David's been working in investment banking for 25 years.
The last ten years of those have been just in marketing services.
So extremely experienced guy to have on our team, really.
I mean he's the big guns basically.
So most of my team are working on the deal anyway.
But once we get to the big negotiation, we trundle David out and he's able to come in and sort of knock heads together and get the right sort of numbers.
But yeah, myself, as I said, my background is marketing and media.
I've been doing this now for seven years.
I was brought in by a company, a small listed company in the UK, to help them find targets because they wanted to business like the business I'd sold.
And then it just kind of snowballed from there.
So myself and David are heading it up and then we have what we call senior advisors on the team as well.
And so it varies who we bring on, usually an expert in the market.
So for instance, we have heather Fullerton in New York and she works with us quite regularly.
She's been CEO of an agency, a couple of agencies and COO as well herself and been through several buyouts.
So extremely experienced.
And we've got Andy Hart in the UK who is vice president, Microsoft Europe.
So again, extremely experienced buying and selling businesses.
So yeah, that's pretty much it.
Who would be or who might be our kind of regular day to day contact.
And what is the cadence of communication during this six month process?
So it's likely to be either Jack, based in London, or Ramon, based in New York.
So they will.
Yeah, they'll manage the day to day stuff.
The way it works is I'll give you a sort of brief timeline overview.
So we have.
Once we sign the engagement letter, we have a kickoff call, basically that's the deal team.
We'll just have a sort of real drill down into the business just to understand it.

It's an hour long, maybe a bit longer, hour long call and after that there's some requests which come on email straight after and they're looking for financial stuff or maybe some other things that wasn't clear.

And then they will take about one or two weeks to sort of get into that and work out evaluation for the business and start putting together your SIM or Im, it's sometimes called which an information memorandum.
And then they'll make some more requests for marketing materials and things.
By the time we get to week four, we should be up and running and ready to go out to market.
And then we book in a weekly meeting with you and your team.
So once we start to get some responses, we're having a weekly meeting with you to make sure we're all on track, running past you.
Any signed NDAs that we've had to make sure that they're companies that you're happy to be introduced to.
Obviously, it's all completely anonymous until we have those signed NDAs.
And then we're, if you're happy, we'll share the iam with the, with a potential buyer.
So yeah, we should be up and running by week four, week five, and then we should have offers on the table by around the third month.
That would be the ideal.
And then 30 days, 36 to 90 days, should I say, of due diligence plus negotiating the contract.
So all in all, it should be about a six month process.
Would you suggest starting now or starting January 1, keeping in mind our year end is January 31.
Yeah, the year end thing, I don't see that's a big problem.
I'm not sure why the other company couldn't get a deal done.
And I mean, there's things that you can do within the, the contract to true up, they call it the numbers at the end of January.
I mean, start February.
They could have just gone back to the numbers and held a small amount of cash that might have changed the deal.
So, yeah, in terms of that, I wouldn't say that there needs to be a delay just because you've not got a complete financial year.
No, I don't mean that.
I just mean by the market.
I mean, we're getting into November now.
Like, is anything done in the month of December by the time we'd be ready to go?
So, yeah, that's a good question.
So it can work two ways.
One way is in your favor.
So if we were to go out to market relatively quickly, actually, sometimes people just want to get a deal done before Christmas.
Other times it's then delayed for three or four weeks by sort of mid December until people are back at work in January and they pick things up.
So it depends.
Sometimes it's good, sometimes it's bad.
That said, you know, we only really have sort of six weeks.
I don't know the exact timings, but six, seven, eight weeks till Christmas.
Eight weeks till Christmas, let's say.
So is that long?
Is that enough to find a buyer?
Potentially it is, but half of that time we're going to be spending just getting your stuff ready.
If we were to wait until next year, it could put us into the second half of next year before a deal is done.
So in my opinion, it's always better to get started.
The sooner the better, really.
Okay.
As long as you're mindful that the deal will pause, the conversations will pause through Christmas and new year.
But that's relatively obvious anyway.
Andy.

Is there any downside to having, like, I'm equating it to real estate, where you've got a stale listing that's been out pre holidays, and then people come back in January and see this as a stale listing versus a new one?
Well, we don't add dates to stuff, but that's a good question.
I really thought that, I mean, we haven't really had a stale listing situation.
Normally, I would say within the first sort of four.
Four weeks of a process, we can get a good read on a business to see if we're going to have a good reaction to it.
But that said, we have had on more than one occasion, we've been through absolutely every contact that we can.
And we started again from the beginning, month, three, four.
We've just gone right back to the beginning and run again, and then found plenty of buyers.
We've also had some sellers that paused the process at six months and come back three months later to try again.
And we found a buyer.
So I don't think in reality they do get stale.
It's just hit.
This is again, going back to the volume play.
Brent, we're constantly out there hitting people's inboxes.
We also do a lot of LinkedIn and some phone calling as well.
It's just you've got to get that in somebody's inbox at the right time for them.
So it's, you know, it might be the right time now, and in six months, the buyer could be ready to go, so.
Yeah, but point.
Point taken.
That's a good way of putting it.
Yeah, that's an interesting way to put it.
Brett, I've never heard of that steal listing before.
Yeah, I don't think, you know, with real estate, because you've got so much volume coming in at the top.
That's not really the way that it happens in reality with what we're doing.
So people aren't going to look and say, these guys have been on listed for six months and they're going to let's go in with a low ball offer.
What I would say is there is an element of that happening in any way.
I mean, that's where you've got to pitch the price really well.
There is an element of buyers that will see what you're listed for and then come under that.
But it happens in both directions as well.
The company we just sold in Israel, for instance, we probably sold for another 50% over the listing price once we got into negotiations.
So it does go in both directions.
Okay, makes sense.
Andy, in my notes for some of your kind of upfront fees, I've got two things that are contradicting, and I think it might have been for the non exclusive.
One, I've got five k for the CIM, but I've also got 30k upfront for the setup.
Was that five k?
Only if we had, like, if it was the non exclusive, like, I can't remember what those.
So the five k is for the valuation.
So we can, we can do evaluation and create the sim for you, and then you can just use that and go to market yourself, including on the agencies platform.
It's free to list on agencies, but for us to run the m and a process is 30k.
So that's the difference and that's in us dollars.
Got it.
Okay.
All right, a couple other questions.
We have some people that have been with us for a really, really long time.
I built the famous, built a business almost like a family.
And so Len and Brent, so we've got some people who aren't going to stick around.
And so we, in our mind, have normalized them out in our adjustment calculations.
Do we need to get rid of some of these people before we start the process so they're not on the books?
Or is that something that we can easily explain to somebody that, you know, these people aren't going to stick around post deal, so we would add them, their salaries back into EBITDA.
What type of roles are they doing, Rob?
